items.title: Madagascar: Southern Africa: El Niño Status and Humanitarian Impacts (October 2026)
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Countries: Madagascar, Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

OVERVIEW

El Niño conditions are underway and are forecasted to strengthen through late 2026, coinciding with a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD).

Key Messages
I. A high-confidence dry season is forecasted for central and southern parts of Southern Africa. Seasonal forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of below-normal rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-normal temperatures, while above-normal rainfall and flooding risks are expected in parts of the northern areas of the region.

II. The region remains highly vulnerable following the severe 2023/24 El Niño, which affected an estimated 54.4 million people and contributed to widespread food insecurity, livelihood losses and disease outbreaks. Currently, humanitarian needs remain elevated, with 11 million acutely food insecure people across the region, while funding levels remain low.

III. Southern Africa experienced one of its largest cholera outbreaks during 2024-25, increasing public health concerns entering the 2026/27 El Niño season.

IV. Governments and partners are advancing contingency planning, preparedness and anticipatory action measures to reduce the expected impacts on food security, water resources, livelihoods, health and protection during the 2026/27 season.

V. Critical funding gaps in preparedness and anticipatory action are undermining efforts to protect vulnerable communities from the expected impacts of El Niño.

items.title: Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) for Riverine Floods – Southwest Region Cameroon
items.author: Christian Blind Mission
items.content:
Country: Cameroon
Sources: Christian Blind Mission, Presbyterian Church, Welthungerhilfe

Please refer to the attached file.

This plan by WHH Anticipatory Humanitarian Action Facility (WAHAFA) partners Christian Blind Mission (CBM) and the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon (PCC) shows how Anticipatory Action supports flood-prone communities in Limbe, Fako Division, Cameroon, to act before severe riverine flooding occurs.

This locally developed Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) combines rainfall forecasts and community observations to trigger early actions addressing health risks, property damage, displacement and food insecurity. Developed with communities, local authorities and organizations of persons with disabilities, the AAP includes drainage clearance, early warning communication and the distribution of water purification tablets, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets and food items.

Using a two-phase trigger mechanism based on forecasts from the National Observatory on Climate Change (ONACC) and local observations of soil saturation, the AAP enables the activation of anticipatory actions with a lead time of approximately 3-9 days and the release of pre-agreed finance from the WAHAFA Fuel funding.

Countries: occupied Palestinian territory, Guatemala, Israel
Source: Islamic Relief

One Year On, Gaza’s ‘Peace Plan’ Has Failed, Delivering More Death, Displacement, Despair – Humanitarian Scorecard

November, 19, 2026

Access the Scorecard

WASHINGTON— One year after an internationally backed ‘peace’ plan for Gaza was launched, it has received a failing score in a scorecard by five leading humanitarian organizations.

The scorecard, led by the Danish Refugee Council, Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International, and Save the Children, gave a score of 4 out of 26 to the Trump administration’s 20-point plan that was endorsed by the UN Security Council. This is down from a score of 5 in a scorecard on the same metrics at the six-month mark in April 2026.

The scorecard assesses progress against the 20-point plan’s own objectives related to civilian protection, humanitarian access, reconstruction and economic development, and freedom of movement and return.

Between the ceasefire declaration in October 2025 and mid-November 2026, at least 1,650 Palestinians were killed and 5,975 wounded, more than double the death toll at the six-month mark. Israeli forces now control up to 70% of Gaza, up from 58% at the start of the ceasefire. The UN has reported near-daily Israeli airstrikes in densely populated areas over the past year.

The ceasefire, which was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803 on 17 November 2025, stipulates an agreed-to minimum of 600 UN-coordinated aid trucks entering Gaza daily. In September, an average of 49 UN-coordinated aid trucks entered Gaza each day with only 2% carrying medical supplies.

Critical shortages of basic medicines and supplies have resulted in deaths from treatable injuries and illnesses. The scorecard, as it did in April 2026, grades humanitarian access in the ceasefire deal with a score of zero.

The Government of Israel continues to obstruct the delivery of shelter materials, medical equipment, and supplies needed to restore water and sanitation services, while nearly the entire population of 2.1 million civilians is struggling to access clean water, healthcare, and adequate food.

All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza remain out of service and not a single hospital is fully operational.

As Gaza faces its fourth winter with little protection from cold and rain, nearly 1 million Palestinians live in sites at medium or high risk of flooding and 89% of households report rodents inside their shelters.

Already this month a rainstorm flooded more than 70,000 tents and a 9-month-old child was reported to have died of hypothermia.

The organizations urge the UN Security Council, the Board of Peace, and Member States to use their leverage to secure immediate humanitarian access and enforce the ceasefire.

Key recommendations include:

  • Lifesaving Aid and Medical Care: Press Israeli authorities to open all crossings, admit essential supplies, lift restrictions on aid operations, and restore medical evacuations and freedom of movement, including the right to return.
  • Aid Oversight: Member States, working with the Board of Peace, should replace Israeli approval and inspection processes with independent, transparent aid verification.
  • Ceasefire Enforcement and Accountability: Member States should establish UN-mandated monitoring and quarterly humanitarian reporting, and use diplomatic, legal, and economic measures to secure compliance with the ceasefire and UNSCR 2803.
  • Recovery and Reconstruction: Member States and the Board of Peace should ensure recovery protects Palestinians’ freedom of movement, prevents forced displacement, and advances commitments under the New York Declaration.

“One year into the so-called ceasefire, Palestinians are still waiting for the safety and humanitarian relief they were promised,” said Jeremy Konyndyk, President of Refugees International. “People are still being killed, Israeli forces are expanding control of Gaza, and families are facing another winter in flooded tents while desperately needed supplies sit just across the border. None of this is inevitable. Israel has clear obligations both under Trump’s peace plan and under international law to protect civilians and allow humanitarian aid into Gaza. The United States and other UN Security Council members must use their leverage to ensure those obligations are met. The commitments made a year ago mean little if they do not change the reality on the ground.”

“The suffering of Gaza’s 2.1 million people is not inevitable. The world must stop accepting it,” said Jan Egeland, CEO of Norwegian Refugee Council. “Palestinians should have the opportunity to recover, rebuild their lives and work towards a better future. But this is not possible unless Israel fulfils its obligations under international law: opening all crossings, allowing humanitarian aid to enter, and ending its unlawful occupation of Palestinian land.”

“One year ago, the world was promised that Gaza’s children would finally see safety, relief and a chance to rebuild their lives. Instead, they are colder, hungrier, more traumatized and more at risk than they were before. This was supposed to be a roadmap out of catastrophe. Instead, catastrophe has deepened. The international community cannot continue to look away. The children of Gaza do not deserve this,” said Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International.

“Regretfully, the Board of Peace failed the international community and continue to ‎provide political cover for ongoing genocide and atrocities. We call on member states ‎‎— especially those with leverage over Israel – to stop issuing plans and take concrete ‎actions: impose an arms embargo, ensure unconditional humanitarian access, and ‎pursue accountability for war crimes. Protecting Palestinian lives and dignity is not ‎only for Palestinians – it is the last line of defense for what remains of our shared ‎humanity and human values,” said Mohsen Abu Ramadan, Board Member of Palestinian NGOs Network.

“The ceasefire in Gaza is failing and Palestinians are still dying, which is a direct result of policy choices made in Israel, the US, and at the UN. Instead of abiding by the ceasefire plan, the Israeli government is continuing its attacks, forcing Palestinians to try and survive without adequate food, water, shelter, or sanitation, amid open sewage and freezing rain – all while the United States does little to stop it. As we have been saying, the government of Israel must allow aid to enter, end its attacks and collective punishment on all Palestinians in Gaza, and allow the long process of rebuilding to begin,” said Abby Maxman, Oxfam America President & CEO.

“A year into the ceasefire, Palestinians in Gaza are being confined as the Yellow Line expands. Israeli forces now control nearly 70 percent of Gaza, and 1.8 million people are squeezed into displacement sites lacking clean water and sanitation. Families that have already fled up to a dozen times are forced to move again when gunfire and explosions erupt, often with no warning. This is displacement by design, and a ceasefire that allows it is a ceasefire in name only. The international community must use its leverage to halt the expansion of the Yellow Line and guarantee Palestinians’ right to return safely to their homes,” said Lilu Thapa, Danish Refugee Council Executive Director Middle East, Asia and Europe.

items.title: Around 700,000 displaced amid volatile conflict in southern Ethiopia, Islamic Relief says
items.author: Islamic Relief
items.content:
Countries: Ethiopia, Kenya
Source: Islamic Relief

Almost 700,000 people have been displaced amid an escalation of conflict in southern Ethiopia along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia border as aid agencies prepare to respond, Islamic Relief says.

The fighting began on 22 October between Somali and Oromo communities, two ethnic groups living in Ethiopia. The epicentre of the conflict is Moyale a border town projected to be increasingly wealthy as trade grows between Kenya and Ethiopia with the two groups fighting for land.

The conflict has spread up to 300km from the town with fighting breaking out in areas across the ethnic group settlements. Approximately 329,000 people have been displaced from the Somali Region Dawa Zone and 359,798 people were displaced across Southern Oromia. Access to the locations has been challenging but aid agencies have had reports that a humanitarian response is necessary.

Hundreds of thousands of displaced people will need support before they can return to their homes. The conflict has caused the destruction and burning of homes, businesses and fuel stations, significant disruption of health, nutrition, water and sanitation services; and civilians are vulnerable to attack.

Approximately 50,000 people have crossed the Ethiopian border into Kenya seeking safety and humanitarian assistance placing additional pressure on local services and host communities.

Islamic Relief Ethiopia head of programmes, Kedir Musema Hameza said:

“This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia. Unfortunately when conflict like this arises it is vulnerable civilians that end up paying a high price. We are seeing that now with this mass displacement of nearly 700,000 people fleeing the violence. This is a serious humanitarian incident which we are working to respond to.”

“Homes have been burnt and peoples lives have been hit. We need funding to respond and help these suffering communities. We have reports from local sources that fighting has stopped and UN teams are travelling to assess the condition of the displaced population and the damage.”

Islamic Relief is working to respond including with cash assistance for affected and displaced people, hygiene kits, community and psychosocial support to communities in conflict hit locations of Ethiopia.

items.title: World toilet day 2026 - Safe toilets, equal futures
items.author: International Organization for Migration
items.content:
Countries: World, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

World Toilet Day 2026 focuses on the connection between sanitation and gender equality. Access to safe, private and dignified toilets is essential to protecting the health and safety of women and girls, supporting their education and livelihoods, and enabling their full participation in society.

Sanitation is foundational to gender equality. By the end of 2025, 82.2 million people were living in internal displacement within their own countries (IDMC, 2026). Many live in camps and informal settlements where sanitation facilities are shared, overcrowded or inadequate. For displaced women and girls, the lack of safe toilets can affect their daily routines, mobility and access to education and livelihood opportunities.

The sanitation crisis affects everyone, but not equally. Unsafe sanitation exposes women and girls to diseases, danger and abuse. In displacement-affected communities, communal toilets without functioning locks, adequate lighting or sex-segregated facilities can compromise privacy and expose women and girls to heightened protection risks, including gender-based violence.

Safe sanitation is a universal human right, and safe toilets mean equal futures. Everyone should have access to sanitation facilities that are safe, accessible, private, inclusive and responsive to their needs. This requires not only appropriate infrastructure, but also meaningful community participation, effective management and regular maintenance.

IOM works to ensure that migrants, displaced populations and host communities have equitable access to safe, dignified and inclusive water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, recognizing their essential role in protecting health, safety and dignity, particularly in crisis and displacement settings. In 2025, IOM reached 5.1 million people with WASH support across 61 countries and territories, including 1.26 million people with safe sanitation (IOM IQBis, 2025).

items.title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs – new research
items.author: Amnesty International
items.content:
Country: Haiti
Source: Amnesty International

Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day.

Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors

Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme

“Survivors of the Kenscoff August attack, which came just weeks after another massacre in the same commune, described how they watched as gang members killed their relatives and friends, and how they were raped, beaten and abducted,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.

“Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors. Survivors must have access to mental health support and necessary protection services.

“On World Children’s Day, we are again calling for the Haitian authorities and the international community to urgently increase efforts to protect Haiti’s children as escalating gang violence continues to threaten their lives. Additionally, intensified security operations must not expose children to further harm.”

World Children’s Day, celebrated annually on 20 November, marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which outlines the rights of every child and what governments must do to protect them. Haiti is a state party to the CRC.

Kenscoff attacks

Organized gangs – namely Grand Ravine, Ti Bwa, 5 Segon and 400 Mawozo – started attacking the mountainous commune of Kenscoff in January 2025. All four gangs are part of the Viv Ansanm coalition.

Kenscoff borders Pétion-Ville, where many government offices, embassies and key commercial interests are situated. The 23 August attack on the population, which began around 9pm and was primarily led by a group from the 5 Segon gang, further appeared to be a retaliation for intensified security operations against the gangs.

One teenage girl told Amnesty International that she hid under her bed as gunshots rang out: “When they came inside the house, they said everybody should get out [or else] they would kill us.”

The girl was abducted and held for a little over one month alongside other abductees: “They [gang members] threatened us a lot… They came in and told us that they didn’t come all this way, risking death, for us to think that nothing would happen to us. They threatened that they would kill us.”

According to the UN, 15 women and four girls were raped. One teenage girl, who was abducted and raped, told Amnesty International: “We heard gunshots, but we didn’t have anywhere to go. We didn’t know where to go… They came in [to our house] and took everybody.”

The girl was tied up with an extension cord and beaten. She was separated from her family, and raped by two gang members on a street: “I tried to fight, but they hit me with a hammer and ripped my underwear… They tied me to a pole and told me they were going to fight with the police… The way they tied me was kind of loose. I freed myself and fled.”

One man who was among the displaced people sheltering in the church said gang members shot and killed one of his family members, a mother of two, as she tried to flee. He managed to hide alongside the two children, but one, a teenage boy, ran to a nearby burial site and was shot. The next morning, the man emerged from hiding and saw that the boy had been shot four times. The boy spent more than two weeks in hospital recovering. The man said of the boy’s condition after the attack: “He has some difficulty adapting at school… he forgets everything.”

Abduction by gangs

Amnesty International documented the abduction of at least 11 children, including three toddlers. Abductees said they were tied up and forced to walk in the dark for hours to houses that gang members had occupied.

Abductees were made to sleep on the floor. One girl said the room where she was initially held was overcrowded, so abductees had to take turns to lie down. They were given very little to eat – mostly crackers, and rice and beans – and untreated water to drink.

Abductees who escaped after security operations faced further hardship and danger as they were caught in resulting aerial attacks, including drone strikes. One girl said she ran barefoot for two days to escape, using her t-shirt to bandage her wounded feet.

The girl said she witnessed at least two boys abducted alongside her die after being injured by the drone strikes. These testimonies are a reminder to Haitian security authorities and their partners – including mercenaries, Salvadoran troops and the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force – of the importance of ensuring that members of the population are spared during security operations.

Witnesses said gang members requested money in exchange for the release of some abductees. Some family members said they simply could not afford to make the ransom payments. At least one family paid close to USD 700 to ensure the release of an adolescent girl, but the gang members didn’t let her go.

On 28 August, UNICEF reported that six children and seven women who were abducted had been released. Others remained in captivity for varying periods, with the whereabouts of some still unknown.

The repeated attacks on Kenscoff have caused multiple waves of displacement. The August attack displaced more than 4,200 people. Interviewees described difficult living conditions in displacement and said many displaced children were struggling to return to school. Insecurity has also disrupted agricultural production in the farming commune.

Community members and Haitian and international human rights monitors criticized the apparent inadequate response of security forces to the attacks.

Need for accountability

Authorities are investigating the Kenscoff violence. They must be transparent about these investigations, and make clear the fate of residents who were caught up in the subsequent security operations.

Previous investigations into various massacres by gangs in recent years have not yet amounted to credible trials. Authorities must ensure that impunity is tackled through independent and impartial investigations that hold to account those suspected of criminal responsibility, including politicians supporting gangs.

“Amnesty International continues to call on the Haitian government and international partners to develop and implement a comprehensive child protection plan, ensuring access to education, healthcare and justice for survivors. Protecting children must be an essential part of any response to Haiti’s security crisis,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.

In the months ahead, Amnesty International will release more outputs based on research conducted between September and November 2026, which included a visit to Haiti and more than 60 interviews. The research is part of the organization’s work on the impact of the crisis on children. Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, violence by armed gangs has escalated significantly in Haiti and has amounted to an assault on childhood.

items.title: Afghanistan: Afghan women call for greater opportunities at Global Open Day with SRSG Fatima | United Nations Peace Operations
items.author: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan
items.content:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan

KABUL- Afghan women leaders, journalists, entrepreneurs and civil society representatives met with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of UNAMA, Rabab Fatima, during a United Nations-supported Global Open Day event in Kabul, calling for greater opportunities and meaningful participation for women in Afghan society.

The event brought together around 50 women's rights advocates, media representatives, business leaders, and community members to discuss the challenges facing Afghan women and girls and exchange ideas on how to address them.

In her remarks, Fatima commended the contributions of Afghan women. "Across the country, I have seen the determination, contribution and leadership of women," she said, emphasising that women do not want to be passive recipients of support but active participants in shaping the decisions and policies that affect their lives.

Participants stressed the importance of ensuring women's meaningful participation in public life, including access to education, employment and other fundamental rights. Their calls come amid continued restrictions on women and girls. As of 2026, an estimated 2.4 million girls remain excluded from secondary education, reversing two decades of progress in expanding access to learning opportunities.

"What will happen to Afghanistan in 20 years without educated women?" asked one participant.

Launched by the United Nations Security Council in 2010, Global Open Day events are held worldwide to promote dialogue between United Nations representatives and women's organizations, raise awareness of women's contributions to peace and security, and support their participation in conflict prevention and resolution.

items.title: Nepal: Au milieu des souffrances causées par les inondations, une clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge contribue à faire naître de nouvelles vies au Népal. | IFRC
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Par Fleur Verwer, IFRC coordinator à l'IFRC pour l’opération d’urgence liée aux inondations au Népal.

---

La clinique d’urgence de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) venait tout juste d’ouvrir ses portes pour la journée lorsqu’une jeune femme enceinte et son compagnon s’y sont présentés. Ses vêtements étaient trempés, elle souffrait énormément et ne savait pas quoi faire.

Se rendre à l’hôpital était impossible : les eaux de crue avaient emporté le pont qui y menait, et elle ne pouvait pas traverser la rivière.

Ayant entendu parler de la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge, elle avait décidé de s’y rendre pour chercher de l’aide.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora était de garde lorsque la jeune femme est arrivée.

« Elle n’avait que 18 ans et ne savait manifestement pas quoi faire. Elle nous a expliqué que sa poche des eaux s’était rompue brusquement la veille », se souvient-il.

Pour le Dr Jora, il était immédiatement évident qu’il fallait agir sans perdre de temps. Après un examen rapide de la mère et du bébé, il a organisé son transfert en urgence vers un centre d’accouchement, où elle pourrait bénéficier d'un suivi médical et accoucher en toute sécurité.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora devant la clinique médicale d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge népalaise à Bidur, où il a travaillé pendant plusieurs semaines après les inondations.

Photo: IFRC

Moins d’une demi-heure après son arrivée, la jeune femme était déjà en route. Le Dr Jora, accompagné d’une infirmière de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) et d’un volontaire, l’a escortée à bord d’une ambulance de la CRN jusqu’à un centre de santé urbain situé à environ 25 kilomètres. Son travail était déjà bien avancé et chaque minute comptait. Une trentaine de minutes plus tard, l’équipe l’a confiée au personnel du centre d’accouchement, s’est assurée qu’elle était entre de bonnes mains, puis est retournée à la clinique.

Trois heures et demie plus tard, une petite fille en bonne santé venait au monde.

Lorsque la nouvelle de la naissance est parvenue à la clinique, un immense soulagement a envahi l’équipe qui avait pris cette première décision déterminante.

Plus tard, une équipe de l'IFRC et de la CRN, comprenant Sachiko Kawase, déléguée Santé de l’IFRC, s’est rendue auprès de la mère et de son nouveau-né pour prendre de leurs nouvelles. Elle a constaté que le bébé était en bonne santé et se portait bien.

Pour accompagner la famille dans les jours à venir, l’équipe a remis à la mère un kit de dignité, comprenant notamment un foulard pour le bébé, ainsi qu’un kit d’hygiène. Cette visite constituait la dernière étape d’une chaîne de soins : du premier examen médical au transport en ambulance, jusqu’à cette visite de suivi, la Croix-Rouge avait accompagné la famille à chaque étape.

Au milieu du deuil, de la douleur et des pertes causés par les inondations, cette nouvelle vie a fait naître une lueur d’espoir.

Un membre de la Croix-Rouge népalaise examine une femme à la clinique, qui a pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes en 24 jours.

Photo: IFRC

Un soutien vital après les inondations

L’histoire de cette jeune mère n’est qu’une parmi tant d’autres qui se sont déroulées à la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge à Bidur.

Après les inondations dévastatrices du 26 août, la ville s’est retrouvée largement coupée des services de santé. Le pont qui reliait l’hôpital public à l’autre partie de la ville a été emporté par la violence des eaux. Les personnes qui dépendaient de cet hôpital pour obtenir des médicaments, bénéficier de soins gratuits ou recevoir une assistance médicale d’urgence se sont soudainement retrouvées sans solution.

Pour maintenir l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels, la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a mis en place cette clinique d’urgence, devenue indispensable.

La clinique n’était pas nouvelle, mais son rôle était plus crucial que jamais. Elle avait été déployée pour la première fois après le séisme de 2015 au Népal. Une fois encore, elle a constitué un maillon essentiel de la réponse, faisant toute la différence entre avoir accès aux soins de santé de base et en être totalement privé.

Au cours des 24 jours de fonctionnement de la clinique, les médecins ont pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes présentant des problèmes de santé très variés : des affections bénignes aux maladies chroniques, comme l’hypertension artérielle et la bronchopneumopathie chronique obstructive, en passant par des cas nécessitant une orientation urgente vers un hôpital.

Des membres de la Croix-Rouge népalaise apportent leur aide à deux personnes touchées par les inondations au niveau de la pharmacie de la clinique.

Photo: IFRC

Soutenir la communauté

Âgée de 17 ans, Isha, volontaire de la Croix-Rouge, était présente dès le premier jour d’ouverture de la clinique après les inondations.

« J’habite juste derrière la clinique. Heureusement, ma maison n’a pas été touchée par les inondations et ma famille est en sécurité. Lorsque j’ai appris que la clinique d’urgence était en cours d’installation, j’ai immédiatement voulu apporter mon aide. J’ai assisté le pharmacien et contribué à alléger sa charge de travail », raconte Isha.

Les volontaires comme Isha n’étaient pas les seuls à se dévouer pleinement. Le Dr Jora, qui a travaillé à la clinique pendant plusieurs semaines, ne s’est pas contenté de soigner les patients : il leur a également prêté une oreille attentive et a été profondément touché par les témoignages qu’ils lui ont confiés.

« Je savais que j’étais là pour fournir des soins médicaux, mais les histoires que les gens me racontaient m’ont profondément marqué. Tant de personnes portaient en elles une immense souffrance. Pas seulement physique, mais aussi émotionnelle », confie le Dr Jora.

Il se souvient notamment d’un homme qui avait subi trois crises convulsives successives, chacune durant plusieurs minutes.

« Il vivait seul et était resté inconscient pendant des heures. Ce n’est que plusieurs jours plus tard qu’il s’est présenté à la clinique. Quand j’ai réalisé qu’il avait dû affronter seul cette situation, sans aucune aide pendant une expérience aussi terrifiante, cela m’a profondément bouleversé. Et ce n’était qu’une histoire parmi tant d’autres. Il y en avait tellement.

« C’est pourquoi j’étais reconnaissant de pouvoir être auprès de ces personnes au moment où elles en avaient le plus besoin », ajoute-t-il.

Isha, 17 ans, qui habite juste derrière la clinique, s’est portée volontaire pour assister le pharmacien dès le jour de l’ouverture de la clinique.

Photo: IFRC

Le chemin vers le rétablissement

La clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge ne représentait qu’une partie de l’intervention menée par la Croix-Rouge. En collaboration avec les autorités nationales et locales, et avec le soutien de la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC), la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a notamment eu recours à des hélicoptères pour acheminer des articles de secours vers les communautés isolées en raison des infrastructures endommagées.

Là où les ponts avaient été emportés par les eaux, les volontaires de la CRN ont aidé les populations à traverser les rivières à l’aide de tuin, de simples nacelles se déplaçant le long d’un câble tendu et permettant de transporter des personnes ainsi que des biens de première nécessité vers l’autre rive, notamment pour se rendre à l’hôpital de district de Nuwakot.

La CRN a également rétabli l’accès à l’eau potable pour plus de 13 900 personnes et fourni des premiers secours psychologiques ainsi qu’un soutien psychosocial à plus de 1 700 autres personnes. À Bidur, elle a été la première organisation à commencer à fournir une assistance financière aux familles dans le besoin.

Derrière cette intervention se trouvait un financement mobilisé presque immédiatement : le jour même des inondations, l’IFRC a débloqué près d’un million de francs suisses (CHF) de son Fonds d’urgence pour les réponses aux catastrophes (DREF). Le lendemain, un appel d’urgence de 25 millions de francs suisses, prévu pour une durée de 24 mois, a été lancé.

Cette durée témoigne de l’ampleur des besoins qui restent à satisfaire. Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
Par Fleur Verwer, IFRC coordinator à l'IFRC pour l’opération d’urgence liée aux inondations au Népal.
---
La clinique d’urgence de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) venait tout juste d’ouvrir ses portes pour la journée lorsqu’une jeune femme enceinte et son compagnon s’y sont présentés. Ses vêtements étaient trempés, elle souffrait énormément et ne savait pas quoi faire.
Se rendre à l’hôpital était impossible : les eaux de crue avaient emporté le pont qui y menait, et elle ne pouvait pas traverser la rivière.
Ayant entendu parler de la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge, elle avait décidé de s’y rendre pour chercher de l’aide.
Le Dr Gyanendra Jora était de garde lorsque la jeune femme est arrivée.
« Elle n’avait que 18 ans et ne savait manifestement pas quoi faire. Elle nous a expliqué que sa poche des eaux s’était rompue brusquement la veille », se souvient-il.
Pour le Dr Jora, il était immédiatement évident qu’il fallait agir sans perdre de temps. Après un examen rapide de la mère et du bébé, il a organisé son transfert en urgence vers un centre d’accouchement, où elle pourrait bénéficier d'un suivi médical et accoucher en toute sécurité.
Le Dr Gyanendra Jora devant la clinique médicale d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge népalaise à Bidur, où il a travaillé pendant plusieurs semaines après les inondations.
Photo: IFRC
Moins d’une demi-heure après son arrivée, la jeune femme était déjà en route. Le Dr Jora, accompagné d’une infirmière de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) et d’un volontaire, l’a escortée à bord d’une ambulance de la CRN jusqu’à un centre de santé urbain situé à environ 25 kilomètres. Son travail était déjà bien avancé et chaque minute comptait. Une trentaine de minutes plus tard, l’équipe l’a confiée au personnel du centre d’accouchement, s’est assurée qu’elle était entre de bonnes mains, puis est retournée à la clinique.
Trois heures et demie plus tard, une petite fille en bonne santé venait au monde.
Lorsque la nouvelle de la naissance est parvenue à la clinique, un immense soulagement a envahi l’équipe qui avait pris cette première décision déterminante.
Plus tard, une équipe de l'IFRC et de la CRN, comprenant Sachiko Kawase, déléguée Santé de l’IFRC, s’est rendue auprès de la mère et de son nouveau-né pour prendre de leurs nouvelles. Elle a constaté que le bébé était en bonne santé et se portait bien.
Pour accompagner la famille dans les jours à venir, l’équipe a remis à la mère un kit de dignité, comprenant notamment un foulard pour le bébé, ainsi qu’un kit d’hygiène. Cette visite constituait la dernière étape d’une chaîne de soins : du premier examen médical au transport en ambulance, jusqu’à cette visite de suivi, la Croix-Rouge avait accompagné la famille à chaque étape.
Au milieu du deuil, de la douleur et des pertes causés par les inondations, cette nouvelle vie a fait naître une lueur d’espoir.
Un membre de la Croix-Rouge népalaise examine une femme à la clinique, qui a pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes en 24 jours.
Photo: IFRC
Un soutien vital après les inondations
L’histoire de cette jeune mère n’est qu’une parmi tant d’autres qui se sont déroulées à la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge à Bidur.
Après les inondations dévastatrices du 26 août, la ville s’est retrouvée largement coupée des services de santé. Le pont qui reliait l’hôpital public à l’autre partie de la ville a été emporté par la violence des eaux. Les personnes qui dépendaient de cet hôpital pour obtenir des médicaments, bénéficier de soins gratuits ou recevoir une assistance médicale d’urgence se sont soudainement retrouvées sans solution.
Pour maintenir l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels, la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a mis en place cette clinique d’urgence, devenue indispensable.
La clinique n’était pas nouvelle, mais son rôle était plus crucial que jamais. Elle avait été déployée pour la première fois après le séisme de 2015 au Népal. Une fois encore, elle a constitué un maillon essentiel de la réponse, faisant toute la différence entre avoir accès aux soins de santé de base et en être totalement privé.
Au cours des 24 jours de fonctionnement de la clinique, les médecins ont pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes présentant des problèmes de santé très variés : des affections bénignes aux maladies chroniques, comme l’hypertension artérielle et la bronchopneumopathie chronique obstructive, en passant par des cas nécessitant une orientation urgente vers un hôpital.
Des membres de la Croix-Rouge népalaise apportent leur aide à deux personnes touchées par les inondations au niveau de la pharmacie de la clinique.
Photo: IFRC
Soutenir la communauté
Âgée de 17 ans, Isha, volontaire de la Croix-Rouge, était présente dès le premier jour d’ouverture de la clinique après les inondations.
« J’habite juste derrière la clinique. Heureusement, ma maison n’a pas été touchée par les inondations et ma famille est en sécurité. Lorsque j’ai appris que la clinique d’urgence était en cours d’installation, j’ai immédiatement voulu apporter mon aide. J’ai assisté le pharmacien et contribué à alléger sa charge de travail », raconte Isha.
Les volontaires comme Isha n’étaient pas les seuls à se dévouer pleinement. Le Dr Jora, qui a travaillé à la clinique pendant plusieurs semaines, ne s’est pas contenté de soigner les patients : il leur a également prêté une oreille attentive et a été profondément touché par les témoignages qu’ils lui ont confiés.
« Je savais que j’étais là pour fournir des soins médicaux, mais les histoires que les gens me racontaient m’ont profondément marqué. Tant de personnes portaient en elles une immense souffrance. Pas seulement physique, mais aussi émotionnelle », confie le Dr Jora.
Il se souvient notamment d’un homme qui avait subi trois crises convulsives successives, chacune durant plusieurs minutes.
« Il vivait seul et était resté inconscient pendant des heures. Ce n’est que plusieurs jours plus tard qu’il s’est présenté à la clinique. Quand j’ai réalisé qu’il avait dû affronter seul cette situation, sans aucune aide pendant une expérience aussi terrifiante, cela m’a profondément bouleversé. Et ce n’était qu’une histoire parmi tant d’autres. Il y en avait tellement.
« C’est pourquoi j’étais reconnaissant de pouvoir être auprès de ces personnes au moment où elles en avaient le plus besoin », ajoute-t-il.
Isha, 17 ans, qui habite juste derrière la clinique, s’est portée volontaire pour assister le pharmacien dès le jour de l’ouverture de la clinique.
Photo: IFRC
Le chemin vers le rétablissement
La clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge ne représentait qu’une partie de l’intervention menée par la Croix-Rouge. En collaboration avec les autorités nationales et locales, et avec le soutien de la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC), la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a notamment eu recours à des hélicoptères pour acheminer des articles de secours vers les communautés isolées en raison des infrastructures endommagées.
Là où les ponts avaient été emportés par les eaux, les volontaires de la CRN ont aidé les populations à traverser les rivières à l’aide de tuin, de simples nacelles se déplaçant le long d’un câble tendu et permettant de transporter des personnes ainsi que des biens de première nécessité vers l’autre rive, notamment pour se rendre à l’hôpital de district de Nuwakot.
La CRN a également rétabli l’accès à l’eau potable pour plus de 13 900 personnes et fourni des premiers secours psychologiques ainsi qu’un soutien psychosocial à plus de 1 700 autres personnes. À Bidur, elle a été la première organisation à commencer à fournir une assistance financière aux familles dans le besoin.
Derrière cette intervention se trouvait un financement mobilisé presque immédiatement : le jour même des inondations, l’IFRC a débloqué près d’un million de francs suisses (CHF) de son Fonds d’urgence pour les réponses aux catastrophes (DREF). Le lendemain, un appel d’urgence de 25 millions de francs suisses, prévu pour une durée de 24 mois, a été lancé.
Cette durée témoigne de l’ampleur des besoins qui restent à satisfaire. Les équipes poursuivent leurs efforts pour renforcer les interventions dans les domaines de l’hébergement, de l’accès à l’eau potable et à l’assainissement, des services de santé, du soutien psychosocial et de l’assistance financière. À terme, l’objectif est d’aider les familles à quitter les tentes et les sites d’évacuation pour rejoindre des logements plus sûrs et durables, tout en leur permettant de retrouver leurs moyens de subsistance.
L’histoire de cette mère et de son bébé illustre ce qu’une assistance apportée en temps opportun peut accomplir. Pour permettre à davantage de familles de bénéficier d'un soutien similaire, nous vous invitons à contribuer à l’appel d’urgence de l’IFRC pour les inondations au Népal.

items.author: International Committee of the Red Cross
items.content:
Country: World
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Statement on the Occasion of the 28th Annual Conference of the High Contracting Parties to Amended Protocol II on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Mines, Booby-Traps and Other Devices, 13 November 2026

In far too many places around the world, everyday activities like driving to the market, walking to school, playing outdoors, cultivating land or herding animals, and even handling ordinary devices entail deadly risks.

Landmines, booby-traps and other devices continue to inflict grave suffering on civilians. They impede access to health-care facilities and other essential services, and hamper humanitarian operations. Even once the fighting has ended, these weapons leave behind long-term explosive hazards that impede the safe return of displaced populations and hinder reconstruction and development.

Year after year, mines, booby-traps and other explosive devices claim thousands of lives. According to the Landmine Monitor 2025, the overwhelming majority of victims are civilians, many of them children – the very people who must never be attacked and must be protected from the dangers of military operations. Last year alone, ICRC teams in 28 countries provided physical rehabilitation services for more than 25,000 people suffering with often life-altering injuries because of mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. Many of those we treat are grappling with debilitating physical injuries that also have psychological and financial impacts.

The ICRC is particularly concerned about the dramatic increase in the use of anti-personnel landmines – both manufactured and improvised – including on the territories of High Contracting Parties.

Anti-personnel mines have indiscriminate effects. The ICRC and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, along with states party to the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, condemn the use of anti-personnel mines by any actor, and the ICRC urges all those who continue to use anti-personnel mines to cease such use immediately. We recall in this connection that High Contracting Parties bound by both the Protocol and the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention are prohibited from using anti-personnel mines in all circumstances. We urge High Contracting Parties to give effect to relevant prohibitions and restrictions in their domestic legislation and military instructions, and to reflect these measures in their National Annual Reports submitted under the Protocol.

In addition, we call on all those who use anti-vehicle mines to step up their efforts significantly to protect civilians against their indiscriminate effects. The ICRC has long called for the rules of international law applicable to such mines to be strengthened to enhance the protection of civilians. An anti-vehicle mine (AV mine) does not distinguish between a military, civilian or humanitarian vehicle. Consequently, AV mines can considerably hinder the delivery of humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations. They can also hamper the return of displaced civilians, the cultivation of valuable farmland and reconstruction efforts at the end of active hostilities. Further steps are needed to effectively address the harm caused to civilians by anti-vehicle mines.

Such steps could include, for example, the High Contracting Parties that endorsed the 2006 Declaration on Anti-vehicle Mines using the opportunity of this Review Conference and subsequent meetings of High Contracting Parties to report on their implementation of the Declaration’s commitments. This could also include confirmation that these commitments are now part of military doctrine and policy.

High Contracting Parties must strictly comply with the requirements of Amended Protocol II and its Annex. Recording, retaining and sharing information concerning minefields, mined areas, mines, booby-traps and other devices, as required by Article 9, is key to the implementation of life-saving measures. Another notable obligation is the removal of mines without delay after the cessation of active hostilities, in line with Article 10. States party to both Protocols II and V can develop a joint system to implement the two Protocols and make the process less resource intensive. Helpful guidance is available in the Technical Annex to Protocol V and in the ICRC’s briefing note on preventing and eradicating the deadly legacy of explosive remnants of war.

Madam President,

Today, the ICRC partners with 20 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, with more than 2,100 staff and volunteers, working alongside communities to help reduce their exposure to the risks posed by mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. This work includes technical support in clearance operations, raising awareness of and promoting safer behaviour, physical rehabilitation services, and support for the social and economic inclusion of survivors.

For the protection of civilians, it remains critically important that Amended Protocol II is universally adhered to. We encourage all High Contracting Parties to redouble their efforts to promote its universalization and we call on states that have not already joined the Protocol to do so without further delay.
